title: What Makes a Directory an Extension

hints.text: An extension is recognised by its composer.json, and the package metadata is read from there: the type has to be typo3-cms-extension (typo3-cms-framework for a system extension), the key is extra.typo3/cms.extension-key, the version is extra.typo3/cms.version or the top-level version field, and extra.typo3/cms.Package.providesPackages lists the Composer packages the extension itself ships — present as an empty object where it ships none.

ext_emconf.php is the deprecated fallback for exactly that metadata, and what decides whether it is read is composer.json declaring both fields rather than either: providesPackages present — as an empty object where the extension ships no Composer packages of its own — and a version in extra.typo3/cms.version or in the top-level version field. Declaring one of the two and not the other still reads the file and still raises an E_USER_DEPRECATED during cache warm-up, which a functional test suite running with failOnDeprecation is usually the first thing to surface; a fixture extension therefore needs a version of its own, and any value does, since nothing evaluates it under test. A Composer installation is unaffected either way — building the package artifact skips the fallback before it is reached.

Declaring both fields stops TYPO3 evaluating ext_emconf.php, which is not the same as being free to delete it: Tailor and the TER read that file, so an extension published there keeps it and keeps its contents in step with composer.json. One that goes nowhere near the TER can drop it.

There is no fallback left: an extension whose composer.json does not declare both the version and providesPackages has an invalid package manifest, and the installation throws InvalidPackageManifestException naming the two fields instead of reading ext_emconf.php. System extensions are exempt, a framework package deriving its version from Typo3Version.

ext_emconf.php is what makes a directory an extension outside Composer — the scan looks for that file — and its $EM_CONF array carries the title, the version, the state and the constraints on other extensions. In a Composer installation composer.json is the authority and the file is TER metadata.

The backend title of an extension comes out of the composer.json description, split on the first " - ": what stands before it becomes the title, the rest the description. An extension whose description is one sentence is listed with that whole sentence as its title.

title: Declaring Tables and Columns

hints.text: ext_tables.sql carries only the delta the schema analyzer needs — the tables and columns TCA does not already describe. It is not a schema dump, and a column TCA defines does not belong in it.
ext_tables.sql declares every table and every column of the extension. Nothing is derived from TCA here, so a column that is missing from the file is missing from the database.

hints: Whatever the migration derives from TCA, it derives from the cached TCA: a Configuration/TCA/ file added or changed on a running installation contributes nothing to typo3 extension:setup until the caches are flushed. The entry that TCA is read from is keyed on the TYPO3 version, the project path and the active package list, so adding a file to a package that is already active does not invalidate it, and the command's own package rescan flushes nothing. A fresh installation has no entry at all and builds TCA from the files, which is why the same command creates everything in one pass there.

The command reports «[OK] Extension(s) ... successfully set up.» either way, so its success is not evidence that anything was created: the only failure it has is an extension key the system does not know, and what the setup itself returned is never read. So typo3 cache:flush comes before it whenever TCA changed, and what it did is checked against the database rather than against the command — SHOW TABLES LIKE 'tx_myext_thing' and SHOW COLUMNS FROM tx_myext_thing through the installation's own client, ddev mysql where DDEV runs it. typo3_schema_lookup does not settle it either, because it answers what TYPO3 would create rather than what the database has.

title: The Files an Extension Is Configured By
hints: Configuration/JavaScriptModules.php declares the import map for an extension's backend JavaScript: a dependencies list of other extensions and an imports map from bare specifier to an EXT: path, with an optional exclude list.
Configuration/Icons.php returns an array keyed by icon identifier, each entry naming a provider (SvgIconProvider or BitmapIconProvider) and an EXT: source path.
Configuration/page.tsconfig is auto-loaded from that path and needs no registration call.

hints.text: Configuration/user.tsconfig is auto-loaded the same way.

title: What Still Runs at Boot, and What No Longer Does

hints.text: Shipping ext_tables.php is deprecated: every active package that has one and is not a framework package raises an E_USER_DEPRECATED when the file is loaded, which is on an uncached request and while the compiled ext_tables cache entry is being written. A request served from that cache raises nothing, so a functional suite running with failOnDeprecation is usually the first thing to surface it. What the file carried has declarative homes: backend modules in Configuration/Backend/Modules.php, backend routes in Configuration/Backend/Routes.php, user settings through ExtensionManagementUtility::addUserSetting() in Configuration/TCA/Overrides/be_users.php, and the record types a page type allows through the TCA allowedRecordTypes option in Configuration/TCA/Overrides/pages.php. System extensions are exempt, being framework packages.

ext_tables.php is not loaded at all. Nothing reads the file and nothing reports it, so an extension that still registers there loses those registrations silently — the backend module, the route or the user setting is simply absent.

hints: ext_localconf.php is what is left for what has no declarative file. It runs on every request, so keep it to registration and out of anything that does work.

title: contentRenderingTemplates and Where Plugin TypoScript Lands
hints: $GLOBALS['TYPO3_CONF_VARS']['FE']['contentRenderingTemplates'][] in ext_localconf.php is a membership list of static-include identifiers and does nothing on its own. Every read of it is one test: while a legacy TypoScript static include is resolved, that include's identifier is looked up in the list, and a hit appends FE['defaultTypoScript_<constants|setup>.']['defaultContentRendering'] directly after it. That is the slot ExtensionUtility::configurePlugin() writes every Extbase plugin's TypoScript into, so a matched entry decides ordering — the plugin configuration lands after the content rendering rather than before it. The identifier is the extension key with its underscores removed plus the include path, as in 'fluidstyledcontent/Configuration/TypoScript/', or the bare key alone for an extension shipping ext_typoscript_setup.typoscript. It is read in SysTemplateTreeBuilder::addStaticMagicFromGlobals(), reached from a sys_template include_static_file row, and in TreeFromLineStreamBuilder, reached from an @import or INCLUDE_TYPOSCRIPT line. Grep the checkout for the key to confirm what else reads it on the branch in hand.

hints.text: The pre-IncludeTree resolver reads it too, with the same membership test: TypoScriptParser while it expands an include, and TemplateService::prependStaticExtra() as each static row is prepended.

hints: So an entry is dead as soon as the include it names is gone, and fluid_styled_content is the live case: it registers that identifier and still ships both Configuration/TypoScript/ and the addStaticFile() call in Configuration/TCA/Overrides/sys_template.php that lets a sys_template pick it. An extension whose TypoScript has moved into Configuration/Sets/ has neither, and no @import of the old path is left either, so nothing can ever match its entries — those lines are a cleanup rather than a defect. Nothing reports them: the key is not deprecated, no changelog entry names it, and fluid_styled_content registers itself the same way, so a deprecation review and the Extension Scanner both pass the file. Site sets are the migration such entries are usually left over from, which is the site-sets hint.

title: How a Distributed Extension Repository Is Laid Out
hints: A distributed extension repository has one unit, and it is the package. The test setup, the build tooling, the CI matrix and the release script all exist to develop, verify and ship that one package, and none of it is deployed anywhere. The question that sorts a project repository into two units — could this be installed into a different project — has one answer here, and it is everything.

What the package supports is the constraint in its composer.json, and every judgment about compatibility is made against that. The version the development setup happens to run is one of the supported majors, not the range: an interface that is deprecated on the newest one is still the interface the code has to call while an older one is supported.

One branch usually serves every supported major. What exists only on the newer one is used behind a check, what the newer one deprecates stays until the older one is dropped, and the file the older one still reads stays with it. A recorded suppression for such a deprecation is the work list for the release that drops that major, not debt that release is waiting on.

extension-repository-dependencies is what is committed and what is vendored, and a lock file committed here pins nothing where it matters while hiding the range that has to hold. extension-repository-tests is the instance the suite builds itself, because there is no installation around the package to run in. extension-repository-installation has the Composer keys that install TYPO3 beneath the package, and the two that fail quietly: app-dir, which is accepted where it is written and then ignored, and a typo3/cms-cli constraint that cannot resolve and names typo3/cms-core as the conflict.

title: What Such a Repository Commits, and What It Vendors
hints: The lock file is not committed. A package states the boundaries it supports and the installing project resolves inside them; a resolution committed here pins nothing where it matters and hides the range that has to hold. What stands in for it is a matrix that resolves per supported version — the lowest and the highest of each supported major — so that green means the declared range is green rather than one resolution of it.

An extension that is also installed outside Composer ships what it needs. Nothing installs its dependencies there, so a library it requires is vendored into the repository and loaded where the class is absent. That copy is a second source of the same dependency: it moves with the declared constraint, or it is a fork nobody bumps.

title: The Instance an Extension Suite Builds Itself
appliesTo: browser tests for a published extension
hints: There is no installation around the extension, so the test setup builds one. The testing framework creates an instance per functional test class from the extensions that test names, and a package below Tests/ is a fixture such an instance loads rather than something the repository ships.

Browser tests belong to the extension here. There is no project around it to own the site they run against, and the development setup that serves that site is part of this repository too — so the configuration, the specs and the command that runs them sit with everything else the package owns.

title: Installing TYPO3 Beneath the Extension Repository
hints: The extension's own composer.json can be the Composer root that installs TYPO3 beneath it: it keeps the type typo3-cms-extension and requires typo3/cms-core. What moves the installation out of the way is config.vendor-dir and config.bin-dir, which are Composer's own keys, plus extra.typo3/cms.web-dir for the document root the installer writes index.php into. The console is then at <bin-dir>/typo3.

extra.typo3/cms.app-dir moves nothing. It is accepted where it is written and reported where it is used: every install and every autoload dump prints «Changing app-dir is not supported any more. TYPO3 application dir will always be set to Composer root directory», whether or not web-dir is set beside it, and extra.typo3/cms.root-dir is answered the same way. So the application directory is the Composer root, which here is the repository itself — config/ with settings.php, additional.php and sites/, and var/ with the caches, the logs, the sessions and a file-backed database, are written into the versioned tree and belong in .gitignore. web-dir is honoured, and only below the Composer root: one pointing outside it is reset to the default with «TYPO3 public path must be a subdirectory of Composer root directory».

typo3/cms-cli is not the root package's to require. typo3/cms-core requires it and pins a major of its own, which has nothing to do with the TYPO3 version, so a root constraint that mirrors the TYPO3 major cannot resolve — and the failure names typo3/cms-core as what it conflicts with rather than the line that is wrong. It arrives as a dependency of the core, and the console binary is there without being asked for.

The extension being the root package changes where it is loaded from. Its package path is the Composer root itself, and its Resources/Public/ is published as a symlink out of the document root and up into that root — so an edit below Resources/Public/ is live after a reload with no build step. Nothing is installed into typo3conf/ext/ in a Composer installation: that directory is empty where it exists at all, and it is not a broken installation. Where public resources land and how they are addressed is public-assets.

title: Where One System Extension Ends and the Next Begins
hints: A system extension names the packages it uses in its own composer.json require. impexp requires typo3/cms-core and nothing else; fluid_styled_content requires core, fluid and frontend. A class from a package not named there works in every core checkout, because the root autoloader loads all of them. It fails in a project that installs the extension without that package. So a patch that reaches into another extension adds the requirement, or stays inside its own.

@internal on a class or a method marks what another extension may not use, whatever the visibility says. A change to it takes no deprecation, and an Important changelog entry rather than a Breaking one where installations used it. So a caller in another extension is a finding in that caller. Nothing checks either boundary: checkComposer compares each extension's constraints against the root composer.json, and no integrity check reads a cross-extension call.

A patch that begins in one extension and adds a class or a method in another has crossed. The addition is the second extension's: its tests cover it, and the hints for its subsystem judge it, whatever the patch is named after. A boundary that really moves is a contract change and says so in its commit message.

title: What Publishing to the TER Requires of an Extension
hints: typo3/tailor is the CLI that talks to the TER REST API, and where it is installed decides where it reads its .env from: bin/tailor looks beside itself, at the project root above its vendor directory, and one level above that. Installed as the extension's own dev dependency, an .env at the extension root is read; installed globally, which is what its own CI examples do at job time, that file is never seen and the token and extension key come from environment variables instead. The file holds the API token either way, so it belongs in .gitignore.

Tailor refuses to package an extension that has no ext_emconf.php, and refuses again unless its version equals the version being released and it declares constraints.depends.typo3. That holds on every TYPO3 version and set-version fails the same way, so an extension published to the TER keeps the file and keeps its version in step, whatever composer.json declares. The extension key itself is resolved from the command argument, then TYPO3_EXTENSION_KEY, then extra.typo3/cms.extension-key — and the last is already required for a typo3-cms-extension package to install at all.

ext_emconf.php names the released version after the release as much as before it, so a published repository and an unreleased one read alike. set-version writes the number into composer.json and into ext_emconf.php, create-artefact refuses to package unless the file matches the version being released, and nothing puts it back afterwards. What tells the two apart is the registry rather than the checkout: typo3_ter_lookup with the extension key answers which versions are published, and a git tag is the release you meant to make rather than the one that is out.

The TER does not refuse a version it already holds — it replaces it. The upload endpoint answers HTTP 201 for a number that was new and HTTP 200 for one it overwrote, and Tailor posts the artefact without asking what is published, so releasing a number that is already out succeeds and silently replaces the artefact people are installing. That is why the registry is asked before the release rather than relied on to reject it.

create-artefact writes the zip into a tailor-version-artefact directory below the current working directory, which is the extension root in the ordinary case, so that name belongs in .gitignore beside the .env.

What the artefact contains is decided by Tailor's own conf/ExcludeFromPackaging.php and never by .gitattributes, so one commit hands the TER and a git archive different file sets: an export-ignore attribute takes a file out of the export and leaves it in the artefact. The list's entries are also interpolated into patterns unquoted — directories matched against the head of the path relative to the extension root, files against the filename — so a top-level directory whose name merely begins with a listed one is dropped while the same name nested deeper survives, and a regular-expression character in an entry keeps its meaning. TYPO3_EXCLUDE_FROM_PACKAGING names a replacement file returning directories and files.
